Female Bombay duck (Harpadon microchir) attain an ultimate total length of 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters], a size that distinguishes this species from the smaller lizardfishes of the genus Saurida found in the same coastal waters. This maximum recorded body length, derived from extensive trawl surveys along the northwest coast of India, places Harpadon microchir among the larger members of the family Synodontidae. In contrast, the total length at which females first achieve puberty is considerably smaller, approximately 16 centimeters [Lp = approximately 16 centimeters]. This early onset of sexual maturation, with individuals becoming reproductively capable at roughly one-quarter of their ultimate length, is a common life-history strategy among short-lived, fast-growing marine teleosts that experience high adult mortality from intense fishing pressure. Field data from the Bombay coast indicate that the transition from juvenile to adult physiology occurs rapidly, allowing females to contribute to the spawning stock early in their lives. This reproductive strategy is likely an adaptive response to the highly seasonal monsoonal productivity pulses that characterize the species' habitat, ensuring that recruitment coincides with peak planktonic food availability for the resulting larvae.

The wet weight of a nascent Bombay duck individual is extraordinarily low, with newly hatched yolk-sac larvae weighing approximately 0.00038 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00038 grams]. This minute initial mass, calculated from the average egg diameter of 0.5 millimeters observed in gravid females, reflects the pelagic spawning mode of the species, whereby millions of small, buoyant eggs are released directly into the water column. The tiny larval size imposes a stringent reliance on endogenous yolk reserves during the lecithotrophic phase, a period lasting only a few days before the mouth opens and the larva must successfully capture its first zooplankton prey. The selective pressures acting at this stage are extreme, with mortality rates exceeding 99 percent during the first week of exogenous feeding, a figure typical of broadcast-spawning marine fishes. This bottleneck has profound implications for population dynamics, as year-class strength is largely determined by the match or mismatch between larval emergence and the spring phytoplankton bloom in the Arabian Sea. Consequently, even minor fluctuations in sea surface temperature can dramatically alter recruitment success for this commercially valuable species.

Female Bombay duck at a total length of 33 centimeters achieve a wet body mass of approximately 1000 grams [Wwi = approximately 1000 grams], representing the typical size at which individuals become fully recruited into the commercial fishery. This weight-length relationship, derived from gonad-somatic index analyses and market sampling data collected over multiple decades, indicates a relatively robust body conformation compared to more elongated lizardfish species. The rapid mass gain from the neonatal stage to this intermediate size underscores the exceptionally high growth rates sustained during the first two years of life. Captive rearing trials at the Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute confirmed that individuals fed on a high-protein diet of small crustaceans and juvenile clupeids can reach this mass within eighteen months under optimal conditions. The energetic demands of such accelerated somatic growth are considerable, requiring a daily food intake equivalent to roughly ten percent of body weight during the most active phase of the juvenile period. This voracious feeding habit explains the species' success as a dominant predator in the midwater pelagic zone of the northeastern Indian Ocean.

The maximum lifespan of Bombay duck is estimated at approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] when the individuals are maintained at a water temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C], which corresponds closely to the mean annual sea surface temperature recorded in the Gulf of Khambhat. This longevity, while modest by teleost standards, is remarkably long for a fish that experiences such intense fishing exploitation, with annual harvest rates exceeding 70 percent of the standing biomass in many years. The recorded age structure in commercial catches is dominated by one- and two-year-old individuals, suggesting that only a small fraction of the population survives to reach the maximum attainable age. Otolith microchemistry analyses performed on older specimens indicate that growth increments narrow considerably after the third year, reflecting a shift in energy allocation from somatic investment toward reproductive output. The 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C] thermal regime appears to be optimal for both growth and gonadal development, as laboratory studies have shown reduced feeding rates and lower condition factors at temperatures above 30 °C. This species' life span of 7 years [am = 7 years] is notably longer than that of the congeneric Harpadon nehereus from the Bay of Bengal, which rarely exceeds 4 years in the wild, likely due to the higher and more variable temperatures experienced in that basin at a temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C].

Field surveys across the species' range reveal that the asymptotic body length of 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters] is rarely attained in modern trawl samples, with most captured specimens measuring between 20 and 45 centimeters, a decline linked to decades of size-selective fishing pressure. Historical records from the 1960s, however, confirm that females measuring 16 centimeters [Lp = 16 centimeters] in total length already exhibit well-developed vitellogenic oocytes during the peak spawning months, indicating that the size at puberty has remained stable despite heavy exploitation. The larval wet weight at hatching is consistently near 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams] across populations, suggesting that stabilizing selection on egg size strongly constrains this trait, balancing fecundity against the likelihood of larval survival in a variable planktonic environment. Interestingly, the body mass of a 33-centimeter female remains close to 1000 grams [Wwi = 1000 grams] even in heavily fished stocks, underscoring the isometric scaling and fundamental canalization of body shape in this species despite rapid demographic shifts and reduced mean age in the population.
